speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Lesage (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):

subtopic: STATEMENT ON MEETING WITH UNITED STATES OFFICIALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to announce that the United States and Canada have agreed on March 19 as the date for a preliminary meeting in Ottawa on the subject of waters crossing the boundary. The meeting will be to establish the agenda and the framework for the discussions.
The U.S.A. group will be headed by a representative of the corps of engineers of the United States army, and it will include three or four officials of the state department.
The Canadian group will be headed by Mr. E. A. Cote, assistant deputy minister of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources, and will comprise two officials of the Department of External Affairs, an official of the Department of Trade and Commerce, and Mr. Lloyd MacCallum, the legal adviser to the international joint commission.

speechtext: May I ask the minister whether any provision is being made for the province of British Columbia to have at least an unofficial representative at this meeting?

speechtext: Would the dominion government have any objection to the province of British Columbia having a member on that committee?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources

speechtext: That is not contemplated at the present time.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON MEETING WITH UNITED STATES OFFICIALS

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: STATEMENT ON MEETING WITH UNITED STATES OFFICIALS
speechtext: I have had discussions with the premier of British Columbia as to the role that representatives of the government of that province might play in the discussions, but there has been no definite request for representation for the purposes of this preliminary meeting dealing with the agenda and the framework of the discussions.

speechtext: May I ask the minister-

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: SUEZ CANAL
subsubtopic: REPORTED IMPOSITION OF TOLLS BY EGYPT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, will the Prime Minister tell

the house the stand of the Canadian government on the latest blackmailing move by Nasser that only ships paying tolls to Egypt will be able to use the Suez canal?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: SUEZ CANAL
subsubtopic: REPORTED IMPOSITION OF TOLLS BY EGYPT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Canadian government knows of no recent blackmailing move by Mr. Nasser. There have been many reports in the news dispatches and over the radio about the reopening of the canal for the passage of ships of not more than 500 tons and about the immediate resumption of work for the removal of the last obstacle in the canal but we have no official information to confirm or to contradict these newspaper reports.

subtopic: SUEZ CANAL
subsubtopic: REPORTED IMPOSITION OF TOLLS BY EGYPT
speechtext: What is the stand of the Canadian government with regard to ships not being able to use the canal unless they pay tolls to Egypt? I ask that question because, as the Prime Minister knows, there was a proposal that half the tolls would be paid to Egypt and half would be paid to the world bank pending settlement. Where does Canada stand in this regard?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: SUEZ CANAL
subsubtopic: REPORTED IMPOSITION OF TOLLS BY EGYPT
speechtext:
Canada
stands here in the House of Commons at this moment, Mr. Speaker. We know that a proposal by the principal users of the canal has been submitted to the Egyptian government and there has not yet been any answer to that proposal.

subtopic: SUEZ CANAL
subsubtopic: REPORTED IMPOSITION OF TOLLS BY EGYPT
speechtext:
What is the position of the
Canadian government? What does the Canadian government think should be done about this question?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: SUEZ CANAL
subsubtopic: REPORTED IMPOSITION OF TOLLS BY EGYPT
speechtext:
I do not
believe that what the Canadian government thinks matters very much until some Canadian ship is required to pass through the canal. The Canadian government does think that the proposal made by the principal users is a reasonable proposal. It is now before the Egyptian government and there has not been any answer yet from the Egyptian government.

subtopic: SUEZ CANAL
subsubtopic: REPORTED IMPOSITION OF TOLLS BY EGYPT
speechtext:
Does the Prime Minister not
think the fact that Canadian taxpayers have already paid $1 million-

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
subtopic: SUEZ CANAL
subsubtopic: REPORTED IMPOSITION OF TOLLS BY EGYPT
speechtext: They loaned it.

subtopic: SUEZ CANAL
subsubtopic: REPORTED IMPOSITION OF TOLLS BY EGYPT
speechtext: -to help clear this canal and also the fact that about one-fifth of the members of the United Nations emergency force are Canadians make it important to the Canadian people what stand the Canadian government takes on this question rather than waiting for a Canadian ship to try to get through the canal?

subtopic: SUEZ CANAL
subsubtopic: REPORTED IMPOSITION OF TOLLS BY EGYPT
speechtext: The Prime Minister thinks that the Canadian government has taken a very wise course in making the sum of $1 million available as a loan to the United Nations for the expenses that have been incurred by the United Nations to hasten the clearing of the canal, and the Canadian government feels that it was an extremely wise move to supply the members of the United Nations emergency force that have been supplied; but the Canadian government does not think that force has gone there to wage war against anyone. It has gone there to try to prevent the resumption of hostilities in the region.

subtopic: SUEZ CANAL
subsubtopic: REPORTED IMPOSITION OF TOLLS BY EGYPT
speechtext:
Perhaps the Prime Minister
will now let us know the stand of the Canadian government with regard to the proposal that no ship may pass through the Suez canal unless it pays tolls to Nasser?

subtopic: SUEZ CANAL
subsubtopic: REPORTED IMPOSITION OF TOLLS BY EGYPT
speechtext: The Canadian government knows of no such proposal. I have just asserted that the proposal of the principal users has been submitted to the Egyptian government and there has not yet been any answer. I do not know whether these news dispatches which have been broadcast this morning are true or untrue. We have no official information about them.

subtopic: SUEZ CANAL
subsubtopic: REPORTED IMPOSITION OF TOLLS BY EGYPT
speechtext:
May
I ask a supplementary question. Will the Prime Minister inform us whether the ships of Israel will have free access to the canal?

subtopic: SUEZ CANAL
subsubtopic: REPORTED IMPOSITION OF TOLLS BY EGYPT
speechtext:
I do not
know. All I know is. what the hon. gentleman knows. There have been news dispatches that all ships that pay tolls to the Egyptian authorities would be allowed to pass.

subtopic: SUEZ CANAL
subsubtopic: REPORTED IMPOSITION OF TOLLS BY EGYPT
speechtext: But not those of Israel.

subtopic: SUEZ CANAL
subsubtopic: REPORTED IMPOSITION OF TOLLS BY EGYPT
speechtext: There was another dispatch, not from the same source, that the ships of Israel would not be allowed to pass. In the face of all these contradictory and unconfirmed reports there is no statement that the Canadian government thinks it is proper to make at this time.

subtopic: ALBERTA
subsubtopic: STATUS OF $22 DIVIDEND PAYMENT
speechtext:
I am afraid you are not quite right on that. As I said, this is highly technical; the basis of payment will have to be determined upon review of the provincial legislation or regulation authorizing payment. As yet, we have no copies of the legislation, but the matter will be considered when that information has been received. So we are holding an open mind; and it is just that it is the business of the national revenue department to keep constantly before them matters such as this as they proceed.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there are just a few remarks I would like to make, and I

was hoping that I might get an answer from the minister to a number of problems before we pass item 1.
One matter on which I should like to get a little information is this. It seems odd that a $2 million tunnel is being built from the C.P.R. station in Vancouver to what I understand is a new $10 million post office.
I was wondering why a tunnel should be built from the C.P.R. station. Why not a tunnel from the C.N.R. station as well, or in place of this one? I was just wondering what the economic arguments are in favour of such a huge expenditure on a tunnel at all. If we take the sum of $2 million even at 4 per cent it amounts to $80,000 a year, and $80,000 a year Mr. Chairman, it seems to me would pay for a lot of trucking of the mail. I am saying this in the light of the fact that nowadays I understand all first class mail is supposed to be taken in by air anyway, and it seems to be merely a matter of a $2 million tunnel to take the newspapers and other second class mail from the C.P.R. station to the new post office. It seems a large sum to the people in the lower mainland, and I am hoping the minister will be able to give the public some of the thinking behind the $2 million expenditure.
I wish to call the minister's attention for one moment to something he said on March 6, as reported at page 1949 of Hansard. I must say, before I put this sentence on the record, that I heartily endorse this sentiment. The minister said:
I was also pleased to hear some hon. members express their satisfaction at the decentralization program which was embarked upon a few years ago and which appears to be working out very well indeed. I might say it is intended that this program be developed further with a view to bringing decision and action as close as possible to the local public.
Now, I do not know what areas of Canada the minister had in mind when he made that statement because I am afraid we in the lower mainland of British Columbia are experiencing the very opposite of what the minister had to say there. We would welcome seeing the implementation of that attitude of decentralization. It seems to us that now that the city of Vancouver is getting a $10 million post office the policy of the department seems to be that all other post offices in the surrounding countryside are supposed to lose their identity and disappear in order to make maximum use of this new Vancouver post office.
The people who are employed in the post offices around the city of Vancouver do not feel at all happy with the trend as they see it developing. Not so long ago the postal employees of New Westminster had to throw
Supply-Post Office
in their lot with the postal employees in the much larger centre of Vancouver. I understand that some representations were made against this policy to the minister, and included among the representations was one representation from the city of New Westminster.
The minister may be able to satisfy certain officials in the city of New Westminster very readily, but there is a good deal of concern over the fact that the post offices around Vancouver are intended to disappear just as rapidly as the services can be replaced by the city of Vancouver. The employees like the personal relationship that exists in the smaller unit. There is no doubt about it that the relationship in the New Westminster post office over the years has been a most happy one, indeed, and we had there loyal and devoted civil servants carrying out their responsibilities, and they did so very ably. Current speculation even is that after the present postmaster and the assistant postmaster there retire New Westminster may even have to do without a new postmaster being appointed.
It is a situation that is causing a good deal of concern. We wish the Vancouver post office well, but we certainly do not like to see all services channelled through that post office, and I must honestly admit that the services we have been getting in mail delivery in the lower mainland since 1953 have declined. I think practically everyone connected with or using the post office will admit that. We found on occasion during the Christmas rush that several blocks of people were denied any mail at all and the only answer they could get was that help simply was not available. First class letters have taken as long as two weeks to arrive at my home from Ottawa. I have those letters on file, and I shall be pleased to send them to the minister. They were properly addressed as Burnaby 1 but were returned with the notation, "Improperly addressed, please re..." or whatever that particular stamp is, that they put on the envelope.
There is another point besides this policy of decentralization that I wish to raise, and that has to do with the size of the four-cent letter rate area. We find it a little difficult to understand why some of the post offices represented in this house by the Minister of Fisheries, which are far removed from the city of Vancouver, should be granted the four-cent letter rate when such relatively nearby places as Port Moody and Port Coquitlam are still being denied the advantage of the metropolitan four-cent rate.
The minister also confirmed our fears in regard to centralization when he replied to the hon. member for New Westminster the other

Supply-Post Office
day. The minister said in regard to the parcel post office service there, as reported at page 1975 of Hansard of March 7:
As I have stated, the idea was to operate throughout the entire Vancouver postal area on a per item basis.
We have been satisfied over the years with the parcel post service as it was supplied to us in New Westminster. I might tell the minister that practically the entire staff in the New Westminster post office is disappointed in the efforts of his department to centralize the whole parcel post delivery service for the entire greater Vancouver area through one Vancouver contractor, namely the Pony Express. I know there may be western politicians who may look with envy at some of the other large Canadian centres where such huge contracts are awarded to only one individual. We see no reason why the parcel post men of New Westminster should not be encouraged to form their own company and submit a bid of their own for that portion of the area they have been serving hitherto. We feel it is not in the interests of good government to award on a contract basis the entire service to one individual who will in turn hire his employees.
I also noticed that the minister seems to be well aware of the offer that was made by the Pony Express to these men at New Westminster, because he supplied us with all the details, not only the minimum income of $1.74 per hour as listed but also some of the conditions of work. I observe that one of the conditions offered to these men was a paid annual vacation of one week in the first year of service. If Mr. Hatch is going to be employing these men I do not see how he can avoid provincial labour laws. He should definitely be subject to the labour laws of the province of British Columbia which call for a minimum of two weeks' holidays with pay. I do not see how he could possibly attempt to offer them only one week paid annual vacation in the first year.
These parcel post carriers do not like to become a part of a big machine nor do mail letter carriers. There is too great a tendency in the world today to make of human beings mere cogs in machines. The postal set-up we have in New Westminster which employs several hundred men is much more satisfactory than when you build up a hierarchy and centralize power in the city of Vancouver.
I realize that my remarks are not going to please the hierarchy of the Vancouver post office because it is only natural that they feel their position is enhanced by the increased number of employees they have and the larger volume of mail they handle and I can well imagine it might be in their own

interests if they could abolish all post offices within 50 miles of that city.
This is a serious matter. I hope the mere fact that the mayor of the city of New Westminster happens to be of the same political affiliation as the government will not be taken as expressing the sentiments of the residents of New Westminster, Burnaby, Port Coquitlam, Port Moody and so on. I do not see any hope for Burnaby at the present time and I trust the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond has more heartening news than I have concerning our eventually obtaining our own post office.
I realize that this thought will be bitterly opposed by the Vancouver post office but we feel that a municipality with between 80,000 and 90,000 people is entitled to a post office. Regardless of the political affiliation of members of parliament who are elected to represent Burnaby in the future, I can assure the minister he is going to continue hearing that demand for at least as long as he is the minister and until he grants our reasonable request.
We have a sub-post office in North Burnaby and one in South Burnaby which are giving very good service, but some of the functions of the sub-post offices have now been moved to the main Vancouver general post office.
We have long asked for a post office in the Edmonds area of East Burnaby. I must thank the minister for the consideration he has given to my previous requests. I used to live in a house on Government road in the Edmonds area in the woods of Burnaby. I wrote a letter and asked for a sub-post office and within a few weeks one was established within a block of my home and so of course I had to write in and thank the minister because I knew it was serving a useful purpose; however, that was not the kind of post office we wanted to see in East Burnaby. Some time later I purchased another home in the outlying area of East Burnaby and I made a similar request. Lo and behold, the Post Office Department obliged and again established a subpost office in East Burnaby only a block from my new home. The people in the Edmonds area of East Burnaby where masses of the people live still do not have the facilities of a sub-post office and I wish that matter would be looked into.
I have in mind another small matter which may not be important to the minister but which is extremely important to the people who want to use the services of post offices. I wonder what kind of arrangements for customer parking have been made at the new Vancouver post office and also at the new post office in New Westminster.

Private concerns erecting buildings in commercial areas of Vancouver or New Westminster nowadays do not receive a building permit unless they make adequate arrangements for parking space to serve the needs of the enterprise or the building they are about to put up. I am afraid the new Vancouver post office will prove to be a severe handicap to automobile owners unless there is adequate parking space adjacent to the building. I think the $2 million that is being spent on the tunnel might more properly have been devoted to arranging for parking space for the customers of the post office.
Concerning the new post office in New Westminster I hope the outside exit door now meets the regulations of the fire marshall and opens to the outside and not to the inside as was the case when the building was opened for business.
The new New Westminster post office has also been built in the centre of a busy commercial area and no parking facilities whatever have been supplied. There are parking metres out in front, of course, but it is rather difficult to find a place to park in a busy area like this and it is a great handicap to people driving automobiles who wish to use the facilities of the post office.
I hope the minister really meant what he said on March 6 when he advised that the post office department has now embarked on a policy of decentralization. This is a most welcome announcement and I hope it will apply all across Canada. I can assure him, however, that on the lower mainland we have seen only more and more centralization and we are much afraid that this tendency will continue unless Ottawa sends out word to Vancouver that decentralization and not centralization is the theme.

Mr. Chairman, in discussing these estimates it is usual for the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam and me to co-operate.
In this case I wish to say something concerning my own part of Burnaby and before I do I would like to express to the minister my sincere thanks for the co-operation that I am receiving from the officials of his department.
I think I can say there has been some contradiction of the views of the deputy postmaster general expressed in this house from time to time, but I am not one of those who subscribe to such views.
I have found that if I make a factual presentation of the requirements of the people whom I represent, although I might not always get an affirmative answer I at least am
Supply-Post Office
given a respectful audience and if it is possible for him to co-operate he does so. That is all a member of parliament can expect from a civil servant.
I should like to direct the attention of the Postmaster General to the situation in South Burnaby. As his officials know, we presently have in service there a postal station which is leased by the department. This was leased over seven years ago at a rental of some $600 or $700 a month. At the time that agreement was made it was quite satisfactory to the people whom I represent in this house. It was something new as we had never had the service before. We got that service through the good offices of the Postmaster General, but with our present increase in population today we believe, having reached the point where there are something like 50,000 people in the southern part of Burnaby, we are entitled to better facilities.
I suggest to the officials of the Post Office Department that a new building be erected there on federal account. This need not be in the same location. The officials of the department would have to indicate their requirements, but a building should be erected on federal account so that the people of South Burnaby may have an adequate postal service, at least for the present.
The situation in Burnaby is a little different from what was outlined by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam. We have to take a long-term view of our postal service requirements. I hope the Postmaster General will consult with his officials and give me an answer to this question. We must consider the situation in Burnaby on the basis of what conditions will be 15 or 20 years from now. I visualize a large public building in central Burnaby to serve the people represented by my hon. friend and me and which could be augmented by postal stations in the three areas, North Burnaby, South Burnaby and what is now known as Burnaby 3 or East Burnaby. My hon. friend and I both had hoped that a postal station would have been provided in the east parts of Burnaby long ago. It has not been done and I hope it will be done this year.
As far as this large federal building is concerned, I would point out to the Postmaster General that there are about 90,000 people in Burnaby. This is the second largest area of population in British Columbia. It seems to both my hon. friend and me that as far as postal services are concerned we are being treated as a poor relation of the new general post office in Vancouver. That is not good enough. Our people have municipal pride and they have postal pride. We think it is about time that a long-term view was taken of the Burnaby situation and proper arrangements were made. I do not expect that it

Supply-Post Office
can be done this year, but certainly the matter should be looked into and a requisition made to public works for a large federal building in central Burnaby to house the sorting facilities and to provide full postal services for the area. As I say, the time is long past when we could be considered as a poor relation of the city of Vancouver. In saying that, I am sure I speak also for my hon. friend.
There are two things I want to ask of the minister. One is that postal plans for Burnaby be considered on the basis of requirements for the next few years, on the understanding that a postal building on federal account will be built in Burnaby at the earliest possible moment. I do not expect the Postmaster General to have this post office in 30 or 60 days, but he should make arrangements for the purchase of the land through public works at the earliest possible moment. I would hope that that could be done this year. I would suggest to him that we do not pay too high a price for the land to speculators who will be most anxious to sell to the federal government. I can assure him that he will receive full co-operation from me in this regard. The land should be expropriated in the first instance.
The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam mentioned a matter which is dear to the hearts of both the hon. member for New Westminster and myself. I refer to the arrangements for the delivery of parcel post. I am quite willing to listen to any facts that may be presented in this connection as I realize that at times members of parliament may not have all the facts. However, it has been represented to me by a delegation representing the men who have been doing this work over the years that they are being put out of work or placed in a different category of possibly working for someone else. Apparently the Post Office Department considers that the Pony Express people in Vancouver can do the job better, but I doubt it. If they can do it more cheaply and more satisfactorily, then I am willing to go along with the idea, because I am of the opinion that even though the Post Office Department has a large surplus they should try to save money. Are the officials of the Post Office Department sure that the Pony Express people are the people to do this work? Are they saving us money? Is the department sure that it is getting the work done better and for less money than it could be done by these little people who have bought cars with which to do this work?
Suggestions were made to me by the delegation representing these men that they can do the work better and for less money than the Pony Express. I hope to have an answer on this matter from the minister. He made a statement in the house some time

ago that the work was being done to the satisfaction of the department and that it was expected that money would be saved. If that is true, then I would certainly support the minister. If it is not true, then I think they should take a second look at the matter and study the needs of these little people who are being hurt most severely.
These men are taxpayers in my riding and in the riding of my hon. friend. Their families are there and they have made considerable investment in facilities to provide the services required by the Post Office Department. Then all of a sudden, without more than two months' notice, they are thrown out of work or told that they can work for some monopoly down in Vancouver. I doubt that anyone in Vancouver can service the New Westminster-Burnaby area better than people who live in New Westminster and Burnaby. As I say, it may be that the facts are entirely different from what I understand them to be. If that is so, then I will go along with the department if they can assure me that they will get better service and will save money. In that case I would have no argument and that is what I have told these people. But I want to be assured by the department that what is being done is in the public interest.
May I go from Burnaby for the moment to the municipality of Richmond. I have no complaints to make here, but I do want to ask a question. I want to say to the Postmaster General that what has been done for this municipality in the postal sense is most satisfactory. One of the finest postal stations on the lower mainland of British Columbia has been provided for these people. I presented this case to the deputy Postmaster General, he took a long look at it and then decided on the advice of his officials that this needed to be done in the public interest. This is a very fine building which is a source of pride to the municipality and I congratulate the department upon what they have done.
Some time ago I wrote to the department regarding rural routes in the municipality and the decision they reached was in conformity with the request I had made that the name of Richmond, British Columbia, should now be the official address of these rural routes.
I am not too sure whether that now applies to the whole municipality in regard to letter carrier rates. If it does, I think the Postmaster General will say so in his reply; and if he does I will be most happy about the whole thing.
I do want to say again that this municipality of Burnaby, represented by my hon.

friend and me, has reached the point in its growth where the Post Office Department has got to take a long look at what has been happening there. They have got to realize, as we do back home, that it is no longer a poor relation of the great city of Vancouver on the coast. We believe we are entitled to be a separate postal entity entirely. We believe that our carriers should work out of Burnaby alone, without any connection with Vancouver at all. The post office officials in Vancouver will argue that the service will not be as satisfactory as it is now, but I would find it most difficult to be persuaded that that is true; I believe we would get just as good delivery, just as good service, if we had our federal building in central Burnaby to service the two constituencies. I believe federal money should be spent in that regard, and that the thinking of the post office department, especially in Vancouver, should be changed. You know, Mr. Chairman, Vancouver is not the hub of the lower mainland of British Columbia; Burnaby is, and we want our recognition now.

Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to delay the committee unduly, but the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam and the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond have again introduced a subject which every one of us from that area is very interested in. In respect to the letting of' contracts, yesterday the minister made a statement which raised one or two questions in my mind, and I have a question to ask in respect thereto: has the contract for the whole metropolitan area been allotted as yet and, if so, when was it allotted and when was the contract submitted for tender?
Another question was raised by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam having to do with the post office in New Westminster and the possibility of its becoming a part of the whole centralized area of greater Vancouver under the jurisdiction of Vancouver post office. As I understand it, on November 28, 1956, the Postmaster General indicated to the city of New Westminster that it was not the intention of the Post Office Department to make New Westminster a sub-post office at this time. His exact words were: "New Westminster is still a staff post office as it was prior to the creation of the Vancouver metropolitain postal area." There is one word in that sentence which disturbs me. It is the word "still". That word would suggest that there is an indication that in the very near future, possibly on the retirement of the present postmaster who is due to retire, I understand, next year, or on the retirement of his assistant within a year or two,
Supply-Post Office
there is a possibility that the New Westminster post office might become a sub-post office of the Vancouver post office, and under its jurisdiction.
I would like the minister to give some assurance that such will not be the case. I realize we have a beautiful building being constructed in the city of New Westminster at this time-a portion of it is already in operation-but it does cause us some concern in the city itself to feel this work might be interpreted to mean that in the not too distant future a change will take place.

On Wednesday, I think, I made certain representations to him which were probably of not much significance as far as the financial side is concerned but which do affect my constituents, and I hope, Mr. Chairman, that before we leave this first item the minister will at least answer my representations in regard to the Torquay mail service and also in respect to the post office accommodation at Maryfield.

Possibly, Mr. Chairman, I could deal with the two points which the hon. member has raised, because I know he has been expecting an answer for the last two days. He did mention to me the question of the postal accommodation in Maryfield where we at present occupy floor space rented by the public works department. Last year we did ask the public works department to find more suitable accommodation-to secure larger quarters-because we had established the fact that the present accommodation is not sufficient to cope with the volume of business. The last report I received from the public works department, which was dated in January of 1957, was to the effect that they had endeavoured to secure accommodation but were meeting with much difficulty. However, they had one of their field men out again trying to make arrangements to secure better accommodation.
As regards the Torquay station where mails are received by train from Estevan on Monday, Wednesday and Thursday, and dispatched on Tuesday, Wednesday and Friday,

Supply-Post Office
we are making inquiries at the present time to see whether a truck service could be established so that mail could be delivered on the days when the train does not provide this service.
The hon. member asked me about the case of rural route No. 1 at Manor. I am sure I will have to look into this further. The route is a long enough one; it covers about 39 miles, with only 51 boxes along the route, which makes a very low average of boxes for such a route. However, the whole matter will be looked into together with many other rural routes, as I have already announced to the house.

wonder, Mr. Chairman, if the minister would give further consideration to the representation I made in respect to the Maryfleld station? Mr. Chairman, I do not rise to register any particular complaint about the Post Office Department as far as my own constituency is concerned. I think the services are generally good and I do not receive very many complaints about the Post Office Department. There are, however, one or two things I should like to point out to the minister and ask his co-operation with regard to them.
First of all, may I thank the minister, together with the Minister of Public Works, for the new public building in the town of Claresholm. We worked for some time on that matter. The post office is not yet open but it is pretty well completed now, with only the finishing touches yet to be done. I am sure that the people of that community will be appreciative of the new building. There are other points in my constituency that I hope will have similar buildings in the not too distant future. However, I think I can say that the government has been fair with that constituency compared with many others.
There are two matters that I rose to speak about particularly. One concerns one of the rural routes about which I have no serious complaint to make but only wish to say that some people oh the route want the service extended. I do not think I should take the time of the house in explaining the matter in detail. I think the best thing I can do is to put the details on paper and let the minister have them. However, it appears that this particular route runs within two miles of some families, one of which is a family of two very aged people. They have to walk two miles to collect their mail from their box on the rural route. Naturally weather conditions sometimes prevent them from getting their mail and they do complain that they fancy that at times it has been tampered with. I do not know whether we should call on the post office officials to extend the service or reroute the route, but I simply ask the minister's co-operation in having his officials look into the problem inasmuch as there is a humanitarian aspect involved in it.
The other matter I want to bring to the attention of the minister is rather important. The minister may have to recollect somewhat the geography of southern Alberta. If he looks at his map he will see that there is quite an area south of Calgary. A railway line runs from Calgary to Lethbridge via what is known as the Alderside branch. There are quite a number of communities and fairsized towns on the Alderside branch,

one of which is my own town of Vulcan, a very substantial community. A lot of business is done there.
Any mail addressed to Edmonton posted in any of these communities along that line somehow or other takes two to three days before it is delivered in Edmonton. The mail used to be picked up by the train but since a more rapid train service is now given by what is known as the Calgary-Lethbridge dayliner the mail is now transported by truck. It is picked up along that route and taken to Calgary. The difficulty seems to lie in the delay of the mail from Calgary to Edmonton. The truck apparently arrives at Calgary late in the day with the mail from all these towns.
We will say, for instance, that the truck arrives in Calgary on the evening of a Monday. It is less than 200 miles from Calgary to Edmonton, but if the mail from all these communities reaches Calgary on the evening of a Monday it is not delivered in Edmonton until Wednesday. That seems to be too long a delay in delivering the mail from these communities addressed to the rather large city of Edmonton. I do not know exactly where the delay occurs but there should not be such a delay.
I can tell the minister that there is what is known as the Canadian Pacific midnight train which leaves Calgary for Edmonton every night. It does not leave at midnight but at 10.30 or a quarter to eleven. I do not know whether it carries mail but if it does not it could. There is no reason why the mail from these communities could not be dispatched on that train which arrives in Edmonton around six o'clock in the morning. Consequently, the mail could be delivered in Edmonton that day. I wish the minister would have his officials look into that matter with a view to remedying the delay.
While I am on my feet, there is one other matter I wish to mention. It does not affect my constituency in particular but does affect second class mail coming to eastern Canada from the west. I think what I am about to say may perhaps be true of most second class mail posted in western Canada. There seems to be quite a delay in its delivery in the east. Not long ago I received some second class mail that took a week less one day to reach me here from the time it was posted in Alberta.
I inquired about that matter of one of the postmasters in Ottawa. I was told that that was second-class mail. I explained to him that the slowest train takes only three days in coming and that I could not quite conceive of any reason why even second-class mail should not be delivered here in three to four
Supply-Post Office
days. He said, "Well, there is sometimes a glut in this second-class mail; it comes with very heavy loads. Well, Mr. Chairman, it might be three days or it might be four days but a matter of nearly a week less one day is, I think, a little bit too long. There are several matters that I should like to draw to the attention of the minister at this time. As the minister knows, the city of Regina has been undergoing tremendous growth in recent years; all sections of the city have enjoyed considerable expansion. We have been faced, of course, with the problem of providing mail delivery service to some of these new areas. A considerable length of time has been taken in satisfying the needs. In some sections of the city there has been-and I think justifiably so-a certain amount of criticism about the failure of the Post Office Department to provide daily mail delivery service.
I understand that there are laid down by the department certain requirements which must be met before delivery service can be commenced. However, I would draw to the minister's attention the fact that, until that mail delivery service is instituted, citizens must go to the main post office and secure their mail through the general delivery wicket. Of course, apart from the fact that

Supply-Post Office
this requirement imposes a great inconvenience on the recipients of mail, it provides a serious bottleneck in the post office itself.
I can recall occasions when I have personally gone into the post office and have noticed a great number of people lined up to get their mail through the general delivery wicket. In most cases these people are lined up simply because the Post Office Department has not seen fit to institute a daily mail service in a particular area. Upon inquiry I have been informed that some of the people in the area have not met the requirements, that they have not supplied their homes with the proper letter boxes and so on. The situation therefore is simply this. A few delinquent people in a district are able to hold up mail service to the majority of the people in the district who have cooperated to the fullest extent. Rather than penalize all the people in the district because of the delinquency of a few, it seems to me that some other method might be used.
If mail service were commenced in a district and there were a number of householders in that district who did not get their mail because they did not have the proper mail boxes on their houses, I am quite sure they would get those boxes on. In other words, if they themselves knew that they were being penalized because of their own neglect, I think the desired results could be obtained. But the present regulations simply mean that a few people in the area who apparently have not met the requirements of the Post Office Department with regard to post boxes and so on are able to hold up the delivery service for the majority of the people living in the area. That is one matter that is of great importance in my constituency.
I have made some inquiries of the minister's department and I must say that I have been a little bit disappointed with regard to the length of time I have been awaiting a reply. I wrote to the Post Office Department some time ago-as a matter of fact, on February 14-requesting information just in order that I would be up to date. Since I have been absent from the city for a few months, I desired to get information as to the present status of some of these outlying areas. I asked what areas are now in receipt of daily mail service and when they may expect to commence receiving daily mail service. To this date 1 have not received a reply from the minister's department. I had hoped that information would be forthcoming before the estimates were brought down.
There is another matter that I took up with the department some time ago-over a month ago, as a matter of fact-and it is something
[Mr. Ellis.1
about which I felt the Post Office Department could have supplied me with information. It seems to me that if I were to make inquiry of one of the services and were to ask for the same sort of information, I would get a reply back in a number of hours. Anybody in the Q.M. stores could give me the information. I wrote to the minister's department on February 5 requesting information. I received from the minister an acknowledgement saying that he was looking into this matter but to this date I have not received any reply. The information I sought was simply this. I asked the Postmaster General if he would be so kind as to inform me as to the issue of clothing and equipment to letter carriers, postal clerks and other classifications of employees within the Post Office Department-it seems to me that there should be some scale of issue-together with the frequency of issue of clothing issued to various personnel in the Post Office Department. I have made a thorough check in my office and I find that to this date I have not received a reply.
It seems to me that is something about which the Post Office Department should have been able to supply information almost immediately. Certainly there must be some basis upon which clothing to letter carriers is issued. I am concerned about this matter because I feel that every letter carrier, every postal clerk and every other classification within the Post Office Department should receive, each and everyone, what he or she is entitled to receive. I have received a number of complaints concerning this matter. I am not satisfied that the scale of issue, such as it is, as laid down by the Post Office Department has been met in all cases. I am anxious to see that every letter carrier and every postal dark receives those articles of clothing to which he is entitled and that we do not have them waiting around for months and months, in some cases for a year or more.
I asked for the information first because I wanted to make sure of the facts. If the minister's department had any information to the contrary, if the reports which I have received were not in accordance with the facts, then I want to give the minister every opportunity to give me the information in order that I might check and ascertain the facts. I have received no reply to my inquiry and to this date, of course, I am not clear in my own mind just exactly what those employees are entitled to. I am anxious to find out. Moreover, I am very anxious to find out whether employees are receiving those items of clothing to which they are entitled.

I think this is a very important matter because it affects the working conditions, the well-being and the morale of the Post Office Department. There are a number of other matters, which I should like to bring up at a later time. But I am anxious to impress upon the minister the importance of facilitating the commencement of daily mail service in those new areas in the city of Regina. I am sure a similar situation exists in other cities in Canada, especially in those cities which are enjoying a great deal of growth.
I am anxious to see something done to facilitate the service to those people. Moreover, I am anxious to know that the post office is doing the right thing for its employees with respect to clothing and equipment to which they are entitled. I wish the minister would bring me up to date and give me the information I have requested in order that we might be able to pursue this matter further.

Mr. Chairman, I have a couple of small points. I may say I have less trouble about post office affairs in my constituency than I have with any other department. The only suggestions I have ever heard from a good many of my people are that they think that the local delivery, or the regional delivery, is too slow as compared with air mail delivery. We can all get letters from Ottawa faster than we can get them from New Westminster, or Bur-naby-Coquitlam, but that is a minor thing. Of course, the major suggestion I hear is that they would like restoration of the two-a-day delivery.
There are two points I wish to raise. One might seem like a trivial affair. It is this. What training is given to the new postmen in the way of how to get along with the dogs in the neighbourhoods? As I watched over the years I have noticed that about nine out of ten postmen seem to be able to go down the street and be on good terms with all the dogs in the neighbourhood, but one postman I remember, not in the city in which I now live, seemed to be bitten by every dog as he went down the street. I was wondering whether the post office gave any kind of special training to new postmen when they are taken on to teach them how to get along with the dogs.
The second question has to do with a much different matter. We heard some discussion in the committee yesterday about the amount of alleged profit on first-class mail, and I know the Postmaster General will have something to say on this particular point. But over the years, and once again last [DOT]
Supply-Post Office
year, in this house we have had the question raised of the cost to Canada of delivering American magazines in Canada. I know this is a very long-standing and very controversial question. I know that when the Bennett government came in they tried to redress this extra cost to Canada of delivering American magazines, and they put on a very unpopular and unwise magazine tax which was immediately taken off by the Liberals when they came back into power, iri 1935 or 1936. Could we be brought up to date as to the relative cost to Canada? We all understand how the general post office arrangements work out under which each country pays its own costs and hands the mail over to the other country and by and large the other country delivers it. That works out very well in almost all categories of mail except in regard to magazines as delivered between Canada arid the United States, because practically none of our magazines are delivered in the United States, and a great flood of American magazines are delivered in Canada. I would appreciate it if the Postmaster General at some suitable time under this item would let us know what is the present situation in regard to the two countries with respect to magazines. How much is it costing Canada in the way of service cost to deliver their magazines over and above what we get in the way of receipts on magazines that we ship to Canada?

I should like to direct the attention of the Postmaster General to a situation in my own city. I do so at this point because I regret to say that I have not been able to arrange a satisfactory adjustment by correspondence with the officials of the department. About a month ago or a little more I received a request from the letter carriers' association local in Kamloops that the inspection of the walks be conducted immediately.
That would be early in February. I was informed that semi-annual inspections were scheduled for March and August in Kamloops and it was their feeling that an inspection carried out in March would not reflect the winter conditions in that area and therefore would not give a proper impression or check of the difficulties encountered by the carriers in winter. The one in August would be a reasonable one for spring, summer and fall; but the one in March would not give 82715-128

a proper impression of winter conditions. They therefore asked that the check be made immediately.
When I passed the request on to the officials of the department, with a summary of the reasons such as I have just given here, I was informed that since the check was to be made in March it was not considered appropriate to advance it by a few weeks, which would have been the difference between the March check and the February check then being requested. I replied that even although it was only a few weeks, in our particular area winter is virtually over- that is the real winter-in early March. The back of winter is broken then, whereas in early February when this request had been originally made we do encounter some quite adverse winter conditions. In the last few years particularly, our worst winter conditions have been occurring from about the middle of December to about the middle of February. We sometimes have blizzard conditions, deep snow drifts, thaws, followed by freezes creating ice, slippery conditions and so on, which are not prevalent during March or at any rate not after the middle of March.
I therefore still feel that if an average impression of the conditions to be encountered by the letter carriers in Kamloops is to be obtained, there should be one check made in mid-winter and one in mid-summer or fall, as the case may be; and that to get a proper impression of winter conditions and a proper check of the time it takes the carriers to get around their routes, a check made in March is of no value. I suppose it is probably too late to do anything about the matter this year because we are now into March, but I urge upon the Postmaster General that he have the matter looked into and discussed with his officials because I am confident that, if a practical look is taken, they will arrive at the conclusion that in order to get a fair average cross-section of the difficulties encountered and the time consumed on these routes, a check should be made in the middle of winter rather than in the middle or at the end of March.

I have made several inquiries of the minister before lunch and I had hoped to receive answers, but there are one or two things I should like to say in connection with this item. There was some discussion about the cost of sending out mail from the various departments. The thing which interests me is that in viewing the operations of the Post Office Department we should consider the services which that department renders for

the other departments of government. Various departments send out mail under their franking privileges and apparently the minister is not prepared to indicate the amount of service rendered to the various departments. I think that should be taken into consideration when ascertaining the surplus of the Post Office Department at the end of the year.
While it is true that this may be only a bookkeeping entry, while it may be only a matter of taking money out of one pocket and putting it into another as far as the government is concerned, I submit the Post Office Department should be credited with the value of the services they render just as though they were handling mail for the general public.
The value of the services rendered to the various departments in the carriage of mail should be credited to the Post Office Department. If that were done I think it would be found that the department would have a sizeable surplus. The difficulty is that when the question of salaries is raised the Post Office Department is prone to say to the employees, "We are not in a financial position to do more for you in the way of wages, overtime and working conditions."
I feel that the only way in which you can arrive at the actual cost of running the department as compared with the revenues of the department is to credit to the Post Office Department the actual amounts being spent on behalf of the various departments of the government. If you do that you will be in a better position to assess the policy of the Post Office Department and pay better wages to the employees of that department.
There is one other matter that I am interested in. In common with many other cities in Canada, we in the city of Regina had a new post office opened just recently, and I am particularly concerned about the facilities within that post office. From what I have been able to ascertain and from my own personal observations I have gathered that while a new building was constructed, to a large extent the old equipment was simply moved from the old post office to the new post office. In other words, while a new building was put up, we are not making the best use of that new available space. Equipment which is out of date, equipment which has been used for many years, was simply transferred to the new building. It seems to me that when new facilities are set up to handle mail, when a new post office is built, if you are to make the maximum use of that new facility you should see that the facilities within the building are in line with the building itself.
While I am subject to correction, I should like to hear from the minister; I should like

to know whether what I say is correct and whether, in line with the new building itself, the facilities within the building are adequate to deal with the dispatch of business within the new post office. As I say, I have simply concluded that to a large extent the old equipment in the old building was simply moved down to the new building and we are perhaps not making the best use of the new facilities in the new post office building in Regina. I should like the Postmaster General to comment on that.

I understand too that as this was considered too short, representations were made to postal headquarters in Montreal in order to have this time extended. I repeat what I just said, Mr. Chairman.

Every citizen is generally given a paid two hours' leave to enable him to do his duty to the state by voting on election day. In a spiritual matter, it seems to me that there should be particular attention given, and I do not know why it should not be possible with regard to those employees to reinstate at least the three quarters of an hour period which they had been allowed before, inadequate as it was. Mr. Chairman, I think the attitude of the minister and the Post Office Department is to be commended with regard to what the minister has said about instituting two services a day for ordinary mail In the larger towns as against improving the rural mail service. I do not know what experience is in eastern Canada, but I know that many rural routes in western Canada only have service twice or three times a week. They are not complaining unduly. They are very grateful for the service. But if there is going to be any extension of the delivery of ordinary mail, apart from delivery to business districts, then I think consideration should be given to the rural areas not only with regard to the matter of rural routes but the many localities that are limited so far as mail delivery is concerned because they only have train or bus service perhaps three times a week.
To say that we should institute twice a day delivery service in the larger centres and leave the rural areas with their limited service I do not think is quite reasonable at this stage. I agree immediately that the situation has changed considerably since the introduction of radio and television whereby country people, for the most part, are able generally to get the news in which they are interested even if they must be delayed in getting their newspapers and letters.
However, in the area from which I come there is another thing that has happened which has also upset the mail service to a considerable degree. I may say that I do not think anything can be done about it. It has to do with the taking off of trains and the Post Office Department being obliged to provide other service different from the service that has been provided for those communities over a long period of time. People perhaps get set in their ways. They are accustomed to going to the post office at regular periods. When they find that the train is taken off and the mail has to come in by some other means it is, quite frankly, rather disturbing.
As I say, I do not know what the Post Office Department can do about it, but when we are considering these things and the services that are provided by the Post Office Department for all of Canada, I think we must keep in mind the type of service that can be provided for these areas whose mail services are quite limited, even with the rural mail services or with the train service to certain communities that are not dependent on rural mail services, but which nonetheless

are just as anxious to have their mail delivered to them regularly and frequently as any other section of the community. As I started out to say at the beginning, I commend the attitude of the minister and the department in keeping in mind the needs of these rural areas.
I am in the happy position this afternoon of being able to say something of a complimentary character to the Postmaster General and his department. I wish to express my gratitude for a little bit of added service, a little bit of added courtesy, that the departments instituted last year. I come from an area, which each year holds a plowing match. It has become the recognized institution of that kind in the province of Manitoba, and it compares favourably with the international plowing match in Ontario.
As a little added incentive last year, in order to work up interest in this plowing match, the association having to do with it approached the department with the idea that they would bring in some historical incident to be associated with this plowing match, and asked the department to provide for a special mail delivery to the plowing match and to have a special stamp placed on the letters so delivered. They had the letters addressed to old Fort La Reine, established by La Verendrye in Manitoba in 1738, on the banks of the Assiniboine river. A special coach was arranged for, with four in hand horse delivery to deliver this mail some seven miles out to the plowing match. In this coach they provided a little of added colour by having the premier of our province and his charming wife dressed up in the clothes, used in the early days, of the stage coach, and they rode in this coach to deliver the mail.
Incidentally, as an added attraction the more sporting boys of the community got the notion that the stage coach should be waylaid along the road. They gathered up a few steeds and on horse back proceeded to overtake the stagecoach. However, they did not have any guns, and there was no shooting. Nevertheless this was a very attractive little bit of added colour to that incident.
I am here this afternoon to say to you, Mr. Postmaster General, that the Portage la Prairie plowing match is extremely grateful to the department and to you for the interest you yourself took in this matter and for making it possible to have this little bit of added colour associated with the provincial plowing match of Manitoba. On their behalf I want to express the appreciation that is felt.

With reference to my previous remarks, the postal service in the lower mainland of British Columbia over the past three years has been getting worse instead of better.

I am enclosing a copy of communication received this day from Vancouver, reporting the time lag of postage deliveries from the district of Coquitlam at Westminster post office to Vancouver of five days.

This spring we had a case of a letter mailed in Sapperton being delivered to the district of Coquitlam in four days.

This is passed to you for your information if it is of any assistance in bringing a better service to the people of western Canada.
Attached to the letter of the clerk is a letter from a company which has lost a considerable amount of money because of the failure of the post office to deliver mail within a reasonable length of time.
I have here the envelope of a letter mailed in New Westminster on December 17 to

1202 Morley Street, Burnaby 1. According to the minister's own statement of a year ago, Burnaby 1 is the legal address of 40,000 people. Stamped on this envelope are the words, "Subject to delay due to incorrect addressing. Your postal address is South Burnaby, B.C." I forget whether it was the present minister or his predecessor who announced that Burnaby 1 was the proper address. This letter addressed to Burnaby 1 and mailed on December 17 was not delivered until December 27, ten days later. I have another letter mailed on December 14 at Vancouver and delivered 13 days later on December 27. I might point out that a distance of only a few miles is involved.
In case the minister thinks only Christmas cards may be subject to delayed delivery might I inform him that the first year I was in this house my wife regularly received the copy of Hansard for Monday on Monday of the following week. Both last year and this year she has had to wait up to three weeks for her copy of Hansard. I have here a copy of Hansard of Thursday, November 29, 1956 which was mailed the following day and delivered on December 17.
I have a first class letter in my hand which was mailed in the House of Commons post office on December 19 and delivered ten days later, on December 29. I have another second class letter mailed in New Westminster on December 11 and delivered to an address in New Westminster seven days later, on December 18. In this case the addressee lived in the same area where the letter was mailed and it would be handled by the same post office.
I feel that the people back home have taken almost as much as they can stand, and that includes all the business firms which rely on the mail service for a portion of their earnings and much of their success in life in terms of business transactions conducted by mail. The mail service is letting them down in the worst possible way.
I would like the minister to produce one small scrap of evidence to show that his announced policy of decentralization is taking effect in the lower mainland of British Columbia. I might point out that we do receive inquiries and complaints about delays and nondelivery, and we follow them up. An investigation is made of every case about which we are told. During the last year the number of complaints which were registered with post offices throughout the country and examined into amounted to 167,000.
When one realizes that we handle 1,680,749,000 letters annually I think he will realize the proportion of complaints is not out of the way. I appreciate the difficulties
facing the minister and the department, but the fact is that this is the fastest growing area in the whole dominion. I met a local mail carrier and he told me that he had 600 homes on his route. I appreciate the difficulty the post office is working under. Several years later he tells me, "They have taken on new men, but even so I still have many more homes to cover than I should have." I realize the predicament the minister is in.
I realize that the standard of living is higher in British Columbia than in other parts of Canada, and that the wages the minister is offering to mail carriers is such that while it may attract many applicants in other areas, in our region the wages are considered comparatively low and the minister is always short of applicants for the positions he is advertising. The wages offered are not regarded as being anywhere near sufficient to permit a married man to maintain a family. The result is that today the department is always short of employees.

I should like to see the day when the wages offered will be sufficiently high to attract enough applicants so the department can be brought up to date, and not have all its mail carriers overburdened by having to service more houses than they should have to service.

I know the department would probably receive some complaints from the rural couriers and perhaps from the postmasters, but at the same time I am sure this could be done, that it would not cost the post office any more money, and that everyone concerned would be home in time for dinner at six o'clock, which is not too late in the day. It happens I don't know whether or not the Post Office Department feels it is ethical; I am not complaining.
I think probably the Post Office Department had complaints last year from some of the tourist houses in Haliburton with regard to discourtesy shown them by individuals on the post office staff. That could quite easily happen, because in the Haliburton office there is a good deal of congestion. They should have had a new post office five or six years ago. Now, Mr. Chairman, with regard to these requests for "shoe leather" increases on the rural routes, I would say first of all that I think there should be an increase of 15 per cent over the whole service. maintopic: THE GOVERNING COUNCIL OF THE SALVATION ARMY, CANADA EAST, AND THE GOVERNING COUNCIL OF THE SALVATION ARMY, CANADA WEST
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when this bill had second reading on Monday afternoon last I was not able to be in the house; therefore at this time I crave the indulgence of the members of the committee to add one further word in the discussion of what I regard, as

the sponsor of this bill, as an important piece of legislation in the interests of the operations of the Salvation Army in Canada.
First of all I should like to express appreciation to all hon. members from every group in this house who, without reservation, supported the principle of the bill we have before us. Nothing I can say at this time I am sure would add to the general appreciation that is felt by people from all walks of life in all parts of Canada for the religious, charitable and social welfare work of the Salvation Army.
As was pointed out by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, who so ably presented this bill in my behalf the other afternoon, the Salvation Army commenced its operations in Canada in the year 1882. It has been a vital part of the religious and social life of the dominion almost from the commencement of the life of this nation in 1867. It is perhaps coincidental that the Salvation Army had its beginning in Canada just at the time the construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway commenced, and it followed across the country in the wake of the C.P.R., reaching the remote parts of northern Canada during the Klondike gold rush. There under the extremely difficult conditions which prevailed it offered spiritual solace to the men who took part in that particular aspect of Canadian development.
The Salvation Army has always been the very essence of practical Christianity. I think its work can best be summed up in the phrase that is often used with regard to it, "soup, soap and salvation". That gets right down to the crux of the matter, particularly when faced with the disturbing social conditions that existed during the pioneer phase of Canadian national development.
More recently the Salvation Army has had larger responsibilities placed upon it as a result of the industrial revolution through which Canada has been passing. As a matter of fact the major reason for the bill before the house at the present time arises from the attempt of the Salvation Army to meet the challenge of the new spiritual and social welfare problems arising out of the impact of rapid industrialization and urbanization.
I can speak with some considerable knowledge of this subject, because my own family has been intimately connected with the work of the Salvation Army since the year 1906, when my father as a young English immigrant to western Canada was befriended by this organization.
There is only one further comment which needs to be made at this time, Mr. Chairman, and it relates to a question that arose on Monday last in the remarks made by the hon.

member for Vancouver East. I noticed in the press that this particular query appeared in the form of a headline. I believe the words were to the effect that a ruling of the Department of National Revenue could kill the Salvation Army.
I believe that particular interpretation and indeed the question itself arises from a misunderstanding. Actually in terms of the definition of the Salvation Army as a charitable and eleemosynary institution there is no uncertainty at all concerning its classification for income tax purposes. It is true, as is the case with other welfare organizations of this kind-the Y.W.C.A., the Y.M.C.A. and other similar organizations-that in some cases the Salvation Army makes a nominal charge for services rendered. This is particularly true in instances of hospitals operated by religious organizations. In the case of the Salvation Army in some instances a nominal charge is made for temporary accommodation in hostel institutions. This is done not as a money-making measure but rather to present a challenge to the individual receiving this particular type of aid, where he might have his self-respect further undermined if the assistance offered him was placed on a purely charitable basis. I do not think there need be any uncertainty at all concerning the clear definition of the Salvation Army as a charitable institution in relation to the activities of the Department of National Revenue.
The hon. member for Vancouver East suggested that some legislative formula might have to be devised, but I am quite certain that the work of this organization has become well established in the minds and hearts of the people of Canada, and that there will be no further need at this time to determine that status by additional legislative measures.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to discuss some of the details in connection with this case I am sure hon. members will not expect me to represent that the parties involved are saints.
However, this is a case which was contested, and it would appear to me that it would be right to give this matter the same treatment that was given to Bill No. 44.
It would appear that trouble in this family developed a number of years ago. The husband appeared, and on being questioned by his own counsel was asked how the marriage had gone. His reply was that in 1947, ten years ago, he had been away working for a lumber company, and when he came home he found, in his own words:
When X came back from that trip my wife was away and the house was empty, and the furniture moved into a garage and she had moved with all the clothing and small articles. There was nobody in at that time.
Some of the questions asekd were:
Q. Did she take the children with her?
A. No, sir.
Q. Have you had charge of the children ever since?
A. Yes.
Q. The four children?
A. Yes.
Q. I understand the children are older today?
A. Yes. Twenty-two, 21, 20 and 17.
Then follow some further questions about the children. But when counsel for the wife cross-examined, he asked about these details, whether in fact the husband had been looking after the children. He was a bit evasive. He said he had, but that he had had some help. He said, "When my kids were on vacation-" I am sure that if the hon. member for Saskatoon were here he would be objecting to the use of the word "kids" in referring to children. The hon. member for Saskatoon had occasion to censure detectives in committee on a number of occasions for referring to children as "kids", and I am sure he would wish to do so in this case with regard to the use of this term before a Senate committee.
But in cross-examination it came out that the social welfare organization in the city of Montreal had been required to take care of the children. So in fact the petitioner in this case would in my view be guilty of perjury, in that he represented that he had care of the children when in fact he had not. I think at some point the Minister of Justice should have a look at this case and decide whose responsibility it is to check these cases

Industrial Relations
of perjury. But when the wife in the case was being questioned by her counsel in connection with the break-up of the home she said, when asked what had happened, that her husband used to come home "at all hours of the night." She said:
He was drunk and that used to get on my nerves. He left me to go to live with another woman.
Well, Mr. Speaker, there is a good deal of conflicting evidence here. The husband said the wife's accusation was not true. Then there was a witness who appeared and who also gave some information which was contradicted very shortly afterwards. When questioned by counsel for the petitioner this woman said that a certain suite had been engaged by a couple. Later when cross-examined this witness said she had not said the suite had been rented by the couple.
I admit there was some evidence submitted by the son on behalf of the father which would indicate, as I said at the beginning, that neither of the parties in this particular case could claim to be a saint, but the point I wish to make is that for five years after these people separated, indeed for ten years, no effort was made by the husband to secure a divorce. It was only last October or November, after the wife had been able to get an appropriate court in the province of Quebec to award her $15 a week, that the husband decided it was time to get a divorce. And it is significant that no effort was made to secure any recent information. The husband gives information that goes back to some time in 1952. He was not sure of what month it was, or what date. He alleges that he found his wife where she was keeping house in the early morning. The wife denies that, of course. The son also alleges that five years ago-he was not sure when it was-he went to visit his mother, but he was somewhat vague in his evidence.
It appears to me, Mr. Speaker, that if you have to go back five years; if there was no attempt made by this husband between 1947 and 1952 to institute divorce proceedings, and if it was only after a Quebec court had awarded the wife $15 a week that action was taken, we should have a look at this case before we decide that a divorce should be granted.
Sometimes when motions of this sort are presented it is argued that passing them would kill the divorce. But I would just refer to Bill No. 44, when a similar motion was carried after the hon. member for Vancouver East had discussed it briefly, and the bill was referred to the appropriate committee as to subject matter.
So I move:
That Bill No. 211 be not now read a second time, but that the subject matter thereof be referred to the standing committee on miscellaneous private bills.
I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that if this motion is carried the members of that committee should examine the evidence very carefully and consider whether there has been perjury in connection with this evidence and, if so, what action should be taken. All the evidence would indicate that a great deal of contradictory information has been placed before us.

He said: Mr. Speaker, this is the second time I have introduced this bill in the house. As I stated at the time of introduction this session, the purpose is to have the political affiliation of the candidate placed on the ballot paper. The reason for this is to do away with some of the confusion that has been apparent on many occasions when we have had two or more candidates appearing on the ballot paper with similar names. I will not mention any specific cases. I think it is common knowledge to all members that there have been many occasions in the past when there has been a great deal of confusion.
I	understand that in one constituency where candidates have already been nominated for the coming election, not only their names but their initials are absolutely similar. This can give rise to a great deal of confusion. The last time I introduced the bill it was pointed out by a good many members that in the House of Commons we have no political affiliations, that we are all members of parliament, and political considerations should not be taken into account. I should like to point out, as I have done on previous occasions, that not only are we listed on the seating plan of the house according to our political affiliation but we also sit in the chamber in groups according to our political affiliation. At the back of Hansard every Wednesday we find that the names of the members are .listed with their constituencies and political affiliations.
I am not going to say any more on the bill. I do not think it needs further explanation. In my opinion a good deal of confusion could be done away with in elections if this amendment were made in the elections act.
