speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member for Wetaskiwin said when he rose to move second reading, this is the second time he has introduced this bill. This is also the second time I have risen to say a few words in support of it. As I recall, last year when the bill was before the house there was a good deal of suggestion that when one gets into the theory of parliamentary tradition, political parties do not exist. That may be perfectly true, but what I failed to see at that time and what I fail to see now is why that should contribute a valid objection to the designation of party affiliation on the ballot if the candidate desires to have it there.
As far as I know there is nothing in our constitutional procedure that specifies that members of parliament shall have a certain occupation, but provision is made on the ballot paper for specifying the occupation of the candidate. Rather than this being a matter of grave constitutional concern, I feel it is a question of simple convenience for the voting public, so they may be able to identify and understand who and for what they are voting when they cast their ballots.
As I am sure most hon. members are aware, a similar provision has been incorporated in the election acts of at least some of the provinces with, as far as I can see, no resulting disintegration of the accepted parliamentary traditions under which the legislatures of the provinces operate. I know it certainly is a cause of serious complaint on the part of many electors in the province of British Columbia every time we have a federal election that the voters are unable to identify the political interests of the candidates from among whom they are called upon to choose. I think that is perhaps of greater concern in large, scattered electoral districts, where many of the electors simply have no opportunity to become acquainted personally with the people who are on the ballot paper.
In some of our constituencies it is almost a physical impossibility for the various candidates to visit all the polling areas or centres. I feel it would be a sound step if provision were made to have, at the request of the candidate, the appropriate political label appear below the name on the ballot paper. I think the point made by the member for Wetaskiwin that confusion can arise when two candidates have similar names is quite valid, but in my opinion there is an argument that is valid even where that is not the case. It certainly has become apparent to me that the voters in my area at least would approve of the same system being followed on federal ballot papers as has been followed now for a good many years on ballot papers in provincial elections.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING PRINTING OF BALLOT PAPERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words in support of the previous speaker and the mover of the motion. In the province of British Columbia we have had for several years now as part of the election act a provision that there should be designation on the ballot paper of the political party one represents. We all believe in democracy and the democratic expression of opinion. A great many people in Canada, and rightfully so, want to vote because they support an individual and not a party. If so, they know the name of the person they want to support. There are also those who want to support a party, and that is also a democratic right and privilege. It very often happens that they do not know the name of the official candidate, and upon occasion we have seen two identical names.
If people want to support an individual as an individual, then they know the person. If they want to support a party and do not happen to know the name of the candidate, they should have the right to learn from the ballot paper who is the representative of that party. That principle has been in the election act of British Columbia now over a number of years, and I have not heard any objection to it. I think it gives truer freedom of expression on the ballot paper.
As far as I am concerned I am most certainly in support of the principle of this motion.

This may seem to be a long bow to draw, but it is not when you consider the fact that when a party member chooses to leave one party to affiliate himself with another he very seldom resigns his seat in the house. members not to obey the party whips, but that in their own case it is some kind of black crime if they do not obey their party whips. But even if, as I say, we have all the appearance of party support, every member of the house acknowledges that his representation in the house is the representation of a constituency without regard to party affiliation in any form, and that he is free in the house to do just precisely what his conscience and lis good judgment dictate that he should do.

2.	What was the population of these bands in 1935, in 1956?
3.	How many of these Indians are in the age groups 6-14 and 16-21?
4.	(a) How many unmarried mothers are there in these reserves and how many children have they?
(b) What assistance, if any, other than family allowances is given these women?
5.	(a) How many acres of land are in each of these reserves?
(b) How much of this land is arable?
6.	How many cattle, horses, sheep, swine and poultry are there on each of these reserves?
7.	What are the average earnings of the heads of families on these reserves?
8.	How much relief has the government provided to each of these reserves during each month of 1956?
9.	Has the department any work and wages programs in these reserves and, if so, what are they?
10.	Are there schools on all of these reserves and, if not, which ones lack schools and what is being done to educate their children?
11.	Have any technical or practical training schemes been put into effect to prepare young Indians to take their place in the labour market?

14.	How many homes have been built on these reserves by the department, and are these houses charged to band funds?

Eight day schools are in operation in the Battleford agency and another is to be constructed in 1957-58 on the Saulteaux reserve. The school population is also served by the
Prince Albert, Duck Lake and Onion Lake residential schools, which enrol some 138 pupils from this agency.
In addition, the department pays tuition for all Battleford agency pupils attending nonIndian schools.
11.	During 1956-57, courses in home economics and industrial arts were given to residents of the Thunderchild, Little Pine-Lucky Man, Poundmaker, Sweetgrass, Moosomin, Mosquito and Red Pheasant reserves. In addition, instruction was given in carpentry, power machinery operation and homemaking.
At the request of the department, a short course in agriculture and homemaking was offered at Prince Albert by the university extension division of the University of Saskatchewan, in co-operation with Prince Albert agricultural society, which was open to residents of Saskatchewan reserves, including the Battleford agency. The cost was borne by the department, whose officials assisted in developing the program. Assistance was also offered to enable students to attend vocational training courses provided under other than departmental auspices.

Desirable qualifications for assistants are a high school education, knowledge of agriculture and stock raising acquired through formal education or practical experience; ability to supervise the Indian population in the operation, care and repair of farm and other machinery and ability to deal with administrative matters related to the affairs of the Indians.
13.	Although section 69 of the Indian Act provides, among other things, for loans to Indians to purchase farm machinery and trucks, loans under this section are not available for housing on reserves at the present time.
As a result of recent amendments to the National Housing Act and the Indian Act, Indians will in future be able to apply for N.H.A. loans for housing construction.
Since January 1, 1930, 18 loans for farm machinery under section 69 have been granted, four on the Red Pheasant reserve, 10 on the Sweetgrass reserve, two on the Little Pine-Lucky Man reserve and two on the Poundmaker reserve. Of these, eight loans have been paid in full, eight are in arrears and two are in good standing.
Few bands in the Battleford agency have sufficient of their own funds available for loan purposes. However, band funds are used to provide housing, seed, feed, etc., to Indians.
14.	From 1950 to 1956, inclusive, 67 houses were constructed on Battleford reserves and of these, 17 were paid for from band funds.
